Unofficial until approved by the

  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  September 27, 2021
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:06 p.m., on Monday, September 27, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met in
Council Chambers and virtually via Zoom.

PRESENT via Zoom:  MAZA, MALONEY, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present in person and via Zoom: City Manager Binnquist, City Attorney Montes,
Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager Stover, City Clerk Myles, Director of Finance
Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director of
Library LohGuan, Marketing and Communications Specialist Nguyen, Director of Community
Development Ho, Principal Planner Lam, Assistant Planner Abrego, Fire Chief Phelps, Police
Chief Parra, Director of Human Resources Ko

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-116

The City Clerk hereby reported that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City Council
being held this evening pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section 54955 and
54956 of the Government Code of the State of California.

READING OF ORDINANCE TITLES
Government Code Section 36934 requires that all ordinances be read in full prior to City Council
taking action on the ordinance. By listing the ordinance title on the Council agenda, Council may
determine that the title has been read.

Action Taken:  On motion of Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER, seconded by Ms. PÉREZ, the City
Council determined that the titles to all ordinances which appeared on this public agenda had
been read, and waived further reading. Hearing no objections, the Mayor so ordered.

Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

PRESENTATIONS

1.  DISCUSSION REGARDING 2021-2029 HOUSING ELEMENT OF THE ALHAMBRA
  GENERAL PLAN – F2M20-37, M2M21-131

  1
9-27-21
   Director of Community Development HO delivered a staff report. In October 2020, the City
  of Alhambra kicked off work efforts related to the development of the 2021-2029 Housing
  Element of the Alhambra General Plan. Alhambra’s Housing Element is updated every
  eight (8) years and aligns with the regional planning effort known as the Regional Housing
  Needs Assessment (RHNA), which is a State mandated process that determines future
  and existing housing needs for all income levels in the community. The City retained
  ECONorthwest to assist with an analysis of the community housing needs for all income
  levels and to strategize ways to respond to and provide for those housing needs. The
  Draft Housing Element was released on August 26, 2021 with the public comment period
  concluding on September 26, 2021. The Council requested an additional update be
  presented after the meeting with the Planning Commission and before submitting the Draft
  Housing Element to the State Department of Housing and Community Development
  (HCD).

  Chris BLAKNEY, of ECONorthwest delivered a presentation on the Planning Commission
  meeting and discussion. On September 20, 2021, ECONorthwest provided the Planning
  Commission with an in-depth presentation and facilitated discussion on the components
  of the Draft Housing Element. After a thorough presentation, comments from the public
  and Commission discussion, the Planning Commission recommended to the City Council
  to direct staff to submit the Draft Housing Element to the HCD with emphasis to prioritize
  revisiting the ADU fee structure to lower barriers for affordable housing; and revisit the
  inclusionary housing allocation and fee structure which are identified in the Housing
  Element as work programs. This evening was the final opportunity for input on the Draft
  Housing Element. It was requested the City Council then direct staff to submit the Draft
  2021-2029 Housing Element to the State of California’s Department of Housing and
  Community Development (HCD) for their formal (60) sixty-day review. After HCD’s review,
  staff would bring forward a finalized draft that would be considered for formal adoption by
  the Planning Commission and City Council in December 2021 and January 2022. HCD
  would issue final certification after the City’s formal adoption process.

  Public Comment:

  1) Cathay LIU spoke regarding her personal difficulties finding affordable ADA compliant
  and specialized housing for her children with developmental and physical disabilities,
  her difficulties in building a day activity room for her children under the ADU guidelines
  in Alhambra, the lack of communication with staff, the overall strict and expensive ADU
  guidelines, and a lack of transparency in the process. She requested assistance in
  reviewing her specific building needs.

  2) John BWARIE, representing the Alhambra Chamber of Commerce, made suggestions
  for zoning changes which would allow for more housing. He also submitted his
  comments via email; which are on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  3) Aide ZELLER spoke regarding the difficult process of constructing ADUs as well as
  the high cost of permits and water meters in addition to construction, and urged
  Council to streamline the process for the ease of residents. She discussed her own
  difficulties in constructing an ADU on her property.

  4) Ari ARAMBULA, expressed concerns regarding the public input and noticing for the
  Housing Element and opposed overdevelopment in the City, particularly in the East

  2
9-27-21
   Main Corridor. She also submitted her comments via email; which are on file in the
  City Clerk’s office.

  5) Lewis MCCAMMON suggested a mid-term progress review by the City Council before
  January 26th on how the goals are being met. He discussed the specific items in the
  Housing Element which should be reviewed by Council and consultants. He went on
  to discuss the Site Inventory in the Element and various vacant properties which could
  be sites of housing development. He went on to suggest alternative uses which would
  also benefit the community. He also discussed the various income levels for housing
  and made suggestions for better distribution of housing and more realistic approaches
  to finding locations for housing opportunities on City owned land.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  The following people requested that the commercial areas along East Main Street
  from Almansor Street to Chapel Avenue be returned to the Central Business District
  and housing allowed there match the CDB, extend housing allowance on East Main
  Street easterly to the city border, and allow for higher densities than currently
  recommended on Valley Boulevard to maximize the available property for housing
  production.

  1)  Javier Mendez, representing Joe’s Garage,
  2)  Albert Alan
  3)  Johnson S. Lin, representing Lin & Assoc.
  4)  Angela Babcock, representing Alhambra Main Street Alliance

  The following people advocated for zoning which would make affordable housing
  more accessible in areas such as the East Main Corridor:

  1) Anthony Dedousis, representing Abundant Housing LA
  2) Paul Talbot

  The following people opposed overdevelopment in the city:

  1)  Olga Alarid
  2)  Veronica Hernandez
  3)  Cliff Bender
  4)  Brad Michaels

  Discussion: Councilmember PÉREZ suggested that staff review the ADU fee
  mechanism and conduct an assessment to compare fees with other cities in an effort to
  streamline the process. She further suggested staff study the City of Glendale’s process
  and collaborate with their team to make adjustments to Alhambra’s process. She also
  suggested that the Housing Element include a 100% affordable housing overlay for
  Alhambra. Mr. BLAKNEY stated that his team and staff would be working together to
  assess what would be most appropriate to implement in the context. Ms. PÉREZ and Mr.
  BLAKNEY went on to discuss the pros and cons of increasing density along the business
  corridor in order to calibrate development standards, such as building height and parking
  spaces, to achieve the desired amount of unit production. Ms. PÉREZ expressed that
  while she appreciated the feedback from the business community, she believed that the

  3
9-27-21
   current standards for the East Main Corridor were sufficient. She referred to the many
  concerns received from residents concerning building height and concluded that further
  densifying was not necessary in that area. She praised EcoNorthwest for equitably
  distributing housing throughout the City and acknowledged that there was a need for some
  density to accommodate housing. She went on to refer to Ms. Liu’s comments as an
  example of the need for more accessible affordable housing, and further citied the
  challenges faced by low-income renters such as long waiting lists and the frustration from
  receiving negative comments regarding affordable housing in the community. She stated
  that while the high RHNA numbers were challenging, she added that the State has tried
  to provide better metrics so that the allocation is fairer. She concluded that she supported
  the Housing Element, expressed hope to better utilize ADUs, better educate the public
  and receive better participation from low-income residents, parents, and other groups who
  had not contributed to the discussion.

  Councilmember MAZA supported the consultant and supported the Housing Element as
  a well-balanced document that addressed the restrictions which have been holding back
  modernized development in underserved areas such as Valley Boulevard. He applauded
  Ms. Pérez’s comments regarding the need to provide information to the public regarding
  the state’s actions. He went on to discuss the public’s concerns regarding density and
  expressed that it was important to confine it to certain areas in the City. He stated that
  SB9 would spread density throughout the City but would also affect R1 neighborhoods
  that the City wants to protect. He went on to discuss the potential impact of SB9 on single
  family residence plots. He supported moving forward with the draft Housing Element as
  written.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed the process of
  adopting the Housing Element, the flexibility to amend it once adopted, and the suggestion
  for a mid-cycle review. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER praised the suggestions to change
  zoning on Valley Blvd as it is a perfect transportation corridor and provides more natural
  movement than on other side streets. She also agreed with suggestions to streamline the
  ADU process and that the City should increase their desired number from 600 to 1000
  due trends such as increased multigenerational family homes, professional children
  continuing to live at home, and the low median income level in Alhambra. She went on to
  discuss the need for housing to accommodate people working from home as well as
  tradespeople working in construction and teachers. She agreed with Ms. Pérez’s
  suggestion for an Affordable Housing Overlay. Ms. Andrade-Stadler discussed the
  development of Valley Blvd. to bring in new businesses and the need to carefully review
  zoning for the East Main Corridor to support the area.

  Councilmember MALONEY also discussed the impact of SB9 and SB10 with Mr.
  BLAKNEY. Mr. BLAKNEY specified that while SB10 would have no impact unless adopted
  by the City, SB9 would allow lot splits in R1 neighborhoods, requires that the property
  owner live in home for 4 years prior, and excludes rental properties. He stated that SB9
  could have an uptake rate that would show annual production outcomes but a study
  conducted by the Turner Center showed that the SB9 uptake rate was relatively low for
  the state and Los Angeles County. He stated that while it would not change the Housing
  Element RHNA housing capacity, but as units were developed it would count to the annual
  reporting to HCD. He added that there was no way to study this outcome as of yet. Mr.
  MALONEY and Mr. BLAKNEY continued to discuss the amendment process for the
  Housing Element. Mr. BLAKNEY specified that the Housing Element was not the
  mechanism for implementing changes but rather the framework to make changes to

  4
9-27-21
   zoning codes and ordinances to enact change.

  Mr. MALONEY also supported streamlining the ADU process and suggested reviewing
  the startup costs and ways to reduce costs to residents, such as providing preapproved
  ADU plans. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed potential zoning code updates
  to rezone industrial areas for adaptive reuse. They continued to discuss the approval
  process of the Housing Element and the feedback to be received from HCD, incorporating
  suggestions from the public, submission to the Planning Commission, and final approval
  by the City Council. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. BLAKNEY went on to address concerns
  regarding the East Main Corridor, the process of the zoning code update, and the East
  Main Corridor study versus the purpose of the framework created by the Housing Element
  and the housing goals submitted to HCD. Mr. MALONEY supported the overall plan to
  have a walkable neighborhood in East Main, supported Mr. McCammon’s suggestion for
  a mid-cycle review of the Housing Element to see progress in the area, supported the
  changes to the Valley Blvd. Plan in an attempt to attract more redevelopment and reuse.

  Mayor LEE discussed the balance the quality of life for residents with the RHNA goals.
  She discussed pedestrian safety as an example of higher density affecting traffic. She
  referred to Ms. Pérez’s comments regarding pursuing input from groups of residents who
  have not previously contributed. She further discussed an increased need for moderate-
  and low-income level affordable housing and questioned the fairness and equity of
  Alhambra’s RHNA goals. She also supported Ms. Pérez’s suggestion to streamline the
  ADU process and stressed the need for transparency and accessibility for the public to
  create ADUs. She stated her concern regarding zoning changes to the downtown corridors
  as they would affect pedestrian safety. She also expressed concerns of the effects of more
  mixed-use structures and higher commercial rent on established local small businesses.
  Ms. LEE and Mr. BLAKNEY also discussed the biannual review of certain programs as
  well as the proposed mid-cycle review of the overall progress. Ms. LEE further supported
  Mr. MALONEY’s suggestion to offer preapproved ADU plans and reiterated the need to
  create more opportunities for residents to provide input. She also discussed her work with
  a senior low-income housing complex and the lack of affordable housing units in recent
  developments nearby.

  Ms. PÉREZ and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed the possibility of contracting with other
  consultants as well as grant funding for implementing programs suggested by the Housing
  Element. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER motioned to approve the draft Housing Element, and
  Ms. PÉREZ discussed the approval process with Mr. BLAKNEY before seconding Ms.
  Andrade-Stadler’s motion to approve.

  Action Taken:  City Council: 1) Provided input on the Draft 2021-2029 Housing
  Element; and, 2) Directed staff to submit the Draft 2021-2029 Housing Element to the
  State of California’s Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for
  formal review. (M2M21-131)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  PÉREZ
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

  5
9-27-21
 2.  2021-2022 STRATEGIC PLAN UPDATE – F2M18-35

  Deputy City Manager STOVER delivered a staff report. On July 12, 2021, the City Council
  reviewed the 2021-2022 Strategic Plan goals and objectives. Following the approval of 13
  goals and 61 objectives, the Council was asked to submit a prioritized list of items to
  enable staff assignments and the allocation of resources. A final list of high priority items
  was provided to the City Council and confirmed. Staff focused on the execution of high
  priority Strategic Plan items and provided a quarterly update of the Strategic Plan
  progress.

  Discussion: Councilmember PÉREZ made two suggestions of items to be added to the
  Strategic Plan. She first reiterated comments made during discussion of Item No. 4 at the
  August 9, 2021 City Council meeting regarding a transition away from the HCDA Citizen
  Advisory Commission to a Citizen Advisory Panel, following the City of Toronto’s model.
  She reported on a presentation she attended regarding this topic. She went on to discuss
  the importance of housing issues in the community and the benefits of such a panel which
  would capture a diversity of thought and be inclusive of underrepresented groups who
  would not typically participate. Secondly, Ms. Pérez made a second recommendation to
  add consideration of creating the position of Chief Innovation Strategist, following the City
  of Glendale’s model. She went on to explain that the position would focus on applying
  human centered design to housing issues as a means of solving issues from a human
  perspective with innovative ideas. She explained that the position was funded through a
  grant received from the Bloomberg Group. Ms. Pérez stated that if the City was not able
  to hire a full-time staff member for this position, then she suggested that existing staff
  members could attend relevant conferences to train in this field.

  Mayor LEE spoke in favor of the Strategic Plan and praised staff for their work. She
  highlighted the recruitment of retail businesses to fill vacant storefronts and boost
  economy, the dog park, and the affordable housing project on Second and Main Street.
  She stated that Council and staff had worked hard to prioritize and reprioritize, and
  suggested that any new additions could be considered in the next fiscal year.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER voiced her appreciation of Ms. Pérez’s comments
  and referred to past community meetings at a church and the Civic Center Library in an
  effort to expand public participation. She expressed hope that once the COVID-19
  pandemic was over, that the City could continue to hold more public meetings to further
  engage the community. She went on to highlight items from the Strategic Plan, such as
  the work with Active SGV on the pedestrian safety zone and bike plan.

  Councilmember MALONEY supported the Strategic Plan and suggested that during the
  next planning session, Council and staff consider organizing larger strategic objectives to
  be accomplished by working on specific tasks rather than every task listed individually.
  He reported that Congressmember Judy Chu was working on appropriations to fund a
  strategic plan and a multimodal bike plan for Alhambra. He went on to refer to Ms. Pérez’s
  suggestions regarding inclusion in public outreach. He suggested conducting more
  community meetings, partnering with community groups, and develop the
  recommendations at the next Strategic Planning Session. He referred to the same
  presentation Ms. Pérez attended and also reiterated the idea and model to address
  community issues and receive input from groups who had not previously participated. He
  expressed interest in the model and increasing ways of participatory democracy.

  6
9-27-21
   Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER referred to Mr. Maloney’s comments and opined that there
  were several Alhambra residents attending CalState Los Angeles who may not be able to
  commit to a board or commission appointment, but may be able to participate on a panel
  and contribute their thoughts to community issues affecting them as students. She
  supported Ms. Pérez’s suggestions.

  Council continued to discuss Ms. Pérez’s suggestions for additions to the Strategic Plan.
  Ms. LEE expressed hesitancy to add a Chief Innovation Strategist as a staff position
  without reviewing its impact on the budget and discussed the upcoming midyear budget
  review with Ms. Stover and Director of Finance LIEU. Ms. LEE stated that she would
  instead support sending existing staff members to applicable conferences or presentations
  to educate them on the innovative concepts which a Chief Innovation Strategist would
  carry out. She also supported further staff presentations on future funding for a full-time
  staff position.

  Council went on to discuss Ms. Pérez’s suggestions regarding a Citizen Advisory Panel.
  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER referred to Ms. Pérez’s suggestion to restructure the HCDA
  Citizen Advisory Committee and referred to previous discussion to allow for the Human
  Relations Commission to assume duties of the HCDA Committee. Ms. STOVER stated
  that Council could discuss that option under Item No. 3 on this evening’s agenda. Mr.
  MALONEY suggested that as a starting point to explore the Citizen Advisory Panel in the
  future, that staff communicate and collaborate with HealthyDemocracy.org, who delivered
  the presentation at the conference attended by Mr. Maloney and Ms. Pérez, about this
  model. He supported adding this as a specific task on the Strategic Plan and not an
  objective. Ms. PÉREZ stated that it would be beneficial for Council to get more information
  because this would be a new approach to the public participation process which would
  remove politics and intentionally bring in different people and perspectives. She continued
  to discuss the City of Eugene, Oregon who also implemented this model. She expressed
  that this would be a heavy workload and that it would not be something that an existing
  commission could handle. Ms. LEE reiterated her suggestion to send existing staff
  members to attend applicable training and conferences and to include the City Grant
  Specialist due to the grant funding aspects of Ms. Pérez’s suggestions.

  Council continued to discuss the recommendations, directed staff to add consultation with
  Healthy Democracy to existing Goal No. 44, directed staff to add a Goal regarding
  Innovation Information for City staff to gain more information or participate in forums and
  to continue to follow grant opportunities online, and directed staff to return with a new
  reprioritized Strategic Plan for discussion at a future Council Meeting.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this informational report.

3.  CONSIDERATION OF ORDINANCES RESTRUCTURING VARIOUS BOARDS &
  COMMISSIONS AND ESTABLISHING THE HUMAN RELATIONS COMMISSION AS
  WELL AS THE HISTORIC PRESERVATION COMMISSION – F2M21-36, O2M21-4791,
  O2M21-4792, O2M21-4793

  Deputy City Manager STOVER delivered a staff report. From February through June 2021,
  in response to objectives identified in the City’s 2020-2021 Strategic Plan, the City Council
  discussed a variety of changes to the City’s current groups including the installation of
  new Boards and Commissions. Throughout the discussions, the Council focused on

  7
9-27-21
   changes that will further support the Council and the needs of the community and enhance
  public participation. Staff requested that the City Council consider first reading of the
  proposed ordinances restructuring changes to the City’s Boards and Commissions,
  including the establishment of new Commissions.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER made suggestions regarding the
  description of the Human Relations Commission following the city of Pasadena’s model
  such as adding language to the purpose of the commission stating “to elevate voices of
  underrepresented” and including law enforcement, undocumented, Asian, Latino,
  LGBTQI, and disabled. She also suggested removing references to CDBG and including
  references to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion to the purpose of the commission.

  Councilmember MALONEY supported the establishment of new commissions, supported
  the change of Environmental Commission to Environmental Sustainability Commission,
  praised staff for their work, and supported Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s recommendations for
  the purpose.

  Mayor LEE and City Manager BINNQUIST discussed the role of the Human Relations
  Commission as an advisory commission and in establishing their purposes and goals. Ms.
  LEE supported Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestions.

  Councilmember PÉREZ offered support of the commissions and the suggestions of
  Council.

  Ms. LEE and City Attorney MONTES further discussed the role of the Human Relations
  Commission and Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestions. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER
  continued to discuss potential goals of the Human Relations Commission and their ability
  to address social issues in the community. Ms. LEE spoke to the importance of Council in
  appointing a diverse group of Commissioners who would best represent the community.
  She also discussed the appointment of minors to commissions as non-compensated
  volunteer positions with Mr. MONTES.

  Ms. PÉREZ suggested including community beautification in the language around
  environmental sustainability. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER supported the Art and Cultural
  Events Commission and the Historic Preservation Commission.

  Action Taken:  City Council, by one motion, introduced for first reading the
  following ordinances, with discussed amendments, entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M21-4791: An Ordinance of the Alhambra City Council
  amending Alhambra Municipal Code Chapters 2.24, 2.27, 2.28, 2.32, 2.34,
  2.35, 2.36 and 23.81 pertaining to existing Boards and Commissions

  Ordinance No. O2M21-4792: An Ordinance of the Alhambra City Council
  Amending Alhambra Municipal Code Adding Chapter 2.38 to create the
  Alhambra Human Relations Commission

  Ordinance No. O2M21-4793: An Ordinance of the Alhambra City Council
  amending Alhambra Municipal Code amending Chapter 2.41 to create the
  Alhambra Historic Preservation Commission

  8
9-27-21
   Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

4.  COVID REOPENING UPDATE: DIRECTION CONCERNING PUBLIC MEETINGS –
  F2M20-33

  Deputy City Manager STOVER delivered a staff report. At the last COVID reopening
  update on September 9, 2021, Council provided direction to staff to continue all City
  Council, Boards and Commission meetings to be held via Zoom through the end of
  September 2021, when the Governor’s order allowing teleconferenced meetings would
  expire. Since then, on September 16, 2021, the Governor of California signed into law
  Assembly Bill No. 361 (“AB 361”), which related to electronic/virtual access to Brown Act
  meetings. AB 361, amended open meeting requirements to permit the legislative body of
  a local public agency to hold virtual meetings during certain emergencies proclaimed by
  the Governor through January 1, 2024. AB 361 would be effective beginning October 1,
  2021. Staff provided information on the elements of AB 361 and sought Council direction
  regarding future Council, Boards and Commission meeting protocols in response to the
  Governor’s signing of Assembly Bill 361 (Rivas, Open meetings: state and local agencies:
  teleconference).

  Public Comment:  Lewis MCCAMMON provided updates regarding COVID
  transmission statistics in Alhambra. He further suggested meetings be held in a hybrid
  model which increased public participation.

  Discussion: Councilmember MAZA suggested continuing to hold public meetings
  remotely until it was proven safe to return to in person meetings. He cautioned unknown
  conditions in the fall which may be exacerbated by cold and flu season and praised staff
  for adaptations to public noticing and communication.

  Councilmember MALONEY agreed with Mr. Maza’s comments with regards to Board and
  Commission meetings and stated that he would be open to a hybrid model for Council
  meetings with Zoom options available to the public, but added that there was no current
  pressing need to change at this time. He stated that he agreed with Mr. McCammon’s
  comments that the Zoom platform has allowed for greater public participation.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed safety improvements under ARPA
  funding such as LED lighting and expanding broadband services. She stated that she
  supported in person meetings in Council Chambers or following a hybrid model if
  necessary.

  Councilmember PÉREZ expressed optimism at the declining cases in Alhambra, stated
  that she would be comfortable holding meetings in a hybrid model provided that staff
  enforce vaccination or negative test requirements. She supported continued use of Zoom
  for public participation. She echoed Mr. Maza’s concerns regarding the impact of fall and
  cold and flu season and urged flexibility to handle any changes. Regarding Boards and
  Commissions, she pointed out that many had 10 members and that therefore it made more
  sense to continue meetings via teleconference.

  9
9-27-21
   Mayor LEE supported a hybrid model while continuing to mask and practice social
  distance per CDC guidelines. She pointed out that some residents were eager to return to
  in person meetings due to lack of familiarity with Zoom. She stated that she felt the hybrid
  model was based in science but added that she would also be open to waiting 30 days
  before changing meeting methods. She stated that each Board and Commission should
  be offered the choice or that they could continue remote meetings until Council also
  returned to in person meetings.

  Council reached a consensus that Board and Commission meetings would continue via
  video/teleconference only. Council continued to discuss the merits of different meeting
  models as it would apply to City Council meetings. Council also debated the need for
  safety measures such as testing and/or showing proof of vaccination status and the
  difficulty in enforcing those measures. Ms. LEE and City Attorney MONTES discussed
  State law allowing for distanced meetings, the extension of a state of emergency, and
  safety provisions other cities made for in person meetings. Council determined that both
  City Council and Boards and Commission meetings would continue via
  video/teleconference only for 30 days, after which Council and staff would review
  progress. As a function of remote participation, members of the public would use the “raise
  hand” feature on Zoom to be recognized for public comment.

  Action Taken:  City Council directed staff to continue public City Council meetings
  via video/teleconference (Zoom and telephone) only; directed staff to continue public
  Boards and Commission meetings via video/teleconference (Zoom and telephone) only;
  directed that staff update meeting participation information to allow for direct participation
  during the meeting; and directed that staff return in 30 days at the second regular City
  Council Meeting October for Council to review progress. No formal vote was required.

RECESS & RECONVENE: Mayor Lee called for a recess at 9:20 p.m. and the meeting
resumed with all Councilmembers present at 9:31 p.m.

5.  PROPOSED PLAN FOR AMERICAN RESCUE PLAN ACT OF 2021 RELIEF FUNDS –
  F2M21-67, M2M21-132

  Director of Finance LIEU delivered a staff presentation, which is available in the City
  Clerk’s office. On March 11, 2021 President Biden signed the $1.9 trillion economic
  stimulus bill which became the American Rescue Plan Act 2021 (ARPA). The emergency
  economic stimulus bill provided fiscal aid to address the COVID-19 pandemic and its
  economic impacts. To support immediate local emergency response, ARPA established
  the Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds (SLFRF), which provided $350
  billion for state, municipalities, counties, tribes, and territories. Of the $350 billion, the
  City of Alhambra would receive an estimated $21.8 million in one-time funding. Staff
  presented to the City Council the proposed plan for use of the American Rescue Plan Act
  of 2021 Relief Funds.

  Discussion: Councilmember MAZA discussed projects related to technology and
  modernization with Ms. LIEU, such as the Network Wiring Project, the Electronic
  Timekeeping Software, and Overnight Parking Permits, and the ways in which these were
  affected by the pandemic or could be utilized in the event of a future emergency. Mr. MAZA
  supported efforts which would enhance customer services for residents. Mr. MAZA further
  discussed the economic analysis of West Valley Boulevard with City Manager
  BINNQUIST.

  10
9-27-21
   Councilmember PÉREZ and Ms. LIEU discussed existing costs related to current
  homeless outreach projects such as the HOME program and staff which fell under the
  Public Health item and the contracted homeless service provider, Los Angeles Centers

  The City developed a Stormwater Master Plan in order comply with the Safe Clean Water

  identify potential opportunities for stormwater projects and prioritize the planning process.

  operations and maintenance, and other related eligible activities.

  program associated with the project after the feasibility study. Councilmember MAZA
  referred to prior discussions related to Story Park and Alhambra Park with Mr. DOLPHIN
  and Mr. RAY, who clarified that this was currently a higher priority due to the catchment
  zone and the amount of flow going through the area. Mr. MAZA supported the study and

COUNCIL COMMUNICATIONS (ANNOUNCEMENTS & FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS) F2M21-7

Mayor LEE and City Attorney MONTES discussed the process in which a city could declare an
Historic District and the process for Historic Context Statement which would include a survey of
properties and then passing an ordinance which declares that properties which meet the historic
context survey are either historic or may opt into historic protection status.

Ms. LEE referred to her comments made during discussion of Item No. 1, and requested that
staff look into working with the Los Angeles County to lengthen crossing signal times to allow
elderly pedestrians sufficient time to cross. She stated that she could initiate a letter to the
appropriate department within the County to support the request for a change. She asked that
should any Councilmembers support her efforts, that they contact the City Manager to sign the
letter. Councilmember PÉREZ supported Ms. Lee’s letter and offered insight from her time
working in the Traffic Division of LA County offices. Councilmember MAZA also offered his
support. Councilmember MALONEY offered his support and referred to other City projects
highlighting pedestrian safety.

Ms. LEE next reported a conversation with Guadelisa Rivera, representing Breathe Free
Alhambra Coalition, and her offer to distribute informational materials regarding the recently
passed smoking restrictions in Alhambra. Ms. Rivera in turn, requested that Council declare a
month in the year as Tobacco Prevention Month. Ms. LEE requested that Council approve a
declaration of either October or November as Tobacco Prevention Month. City Manager
BINNQUIST stated that staff could provide a community calendar and suggest an appropriate
month. Mr. MAZA, Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER, and Mr. MALONEY supported Ms.
Lee’s suggestion. Ms. PÉREZ supported Ms. Lee’s suggestion, and stated that there might be an
appropriate month already recognized nationally.

Ms. PÉREZ briefly highlighted Strategic Plan items such as the Vision Zero Work group, Rent
Stabilization Ordinance, and the Just Cause Eviction Ordinance. Ms. PÉREZ and Ms.
BINNQUIST discussed the prioritization of Strategic Plan items and when staff would be able to
create a timeline for working on the items and engage population through outreach.

Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested creating a position for or a contract with a Sustainability
Analyst to assist in creating a separate Sustainability Strategic Plan. Referring to previous
comments, she also reported that World No Tobacco Day is held on May 31, 2022. Ms. LEE
suggested that perhaps May could be declared Tobacco Prevention Month.
